goal_text: How to choose between RAG and fine-tuning

nodes.title: What is RAG, actually?
nodes.one_liner: How retrieval feeds a model external knowledge at query time.

nodes.title: What is fine-tuning, actually?
nodes.one_liner: How training reshapes a model's behavior and built-in knowledge.

nodes.title: What each is good at (and bad at)
nodes.one_liner: Core strengths and weaknesses of each approach, side by side.

nodes.title: How often does your information change?
nodes.one_liner: Why data freshness pushes you toward RAG or fine-tuning.

nodes.title: What data do you actually have?
nodes.one_liner: How data type and volume determine which is feasible.

nodes.title: Cost, latency, and effort trade-offs
nodes.one_liner: What each costs to build, run, and maintain over time.

nodes.title: A decision checklist for your project
nodes.one_liner: Concrete questions that point you to one answer.

outline.rationale: The user is new to both concepts and choosing for a real project, so the outline opens with two foundational definition nodes (RAG, fine-tuning) framed as plain-language questions, then a comparison node establishing strengths/weaknesses. The middle three nodes are the practical decision criteria the confirmed understanding prioritized—data freshness, available data, and cost/latency/effort—kept MECE by splitting the "criteria that matter" into distinct axes rather than one blob. The final node synthesizes into an applicable checklist, matching the "framework I can apply to my situation" goal. Excluded: history/theory, implementation tutorials, and hybrid setups, all explicitly deprioritized. Depth stays at informed-decision-maker level throughout.
